lessons.title: Docker, cloud deployment and LLMOps
lessons.summary: Ship an AI service reliably: containers, CI/CD with eval gates, logging and tracing, provider failures, cost and p95 latency, with a runbook.
keyPoints: Multi-stage, pinned, non-root images with exec-form CMD; secrets come from the environment at runtime, never from the image.
Liveness checks the process; readiness checks local dependencies and must never call the LLM provider.
Prompt and model changes are deploys: version them, gate them with offline evals, canary them, and roll back all changed artifacts together.
Log metadata (tokens, latency, versions, ids), not raw prompts, answers, secrets or PII; trace each stage as a span.
Timeouts must sum below the deadline; retry only retryable errors with backoff and jitter; a circuit breaker turns slow failures into fast skips.
Decide degradation per feature in advance: search-only for read paths, fail closed for side-effecting agents.
Cost per request is tokens by component times price, multiplied by calls; context size, output length and agent steps dominate.
Reduce p95 by tracing per stage, streaming, parallelising and trimming context, and prove quality held with the eval.

check.q: Why should the readiness probe of an LLM service not call the model provider?
options: Provider calls are too expensive to run every few seconds
During a provider outage every instance would become not-ready at once, removing all targets and turning a partial outage into a total one
Readiness probes cannot make outbound network calls
The provider rate limit applies only to health endpoints
check.why: Provider health belongs in the circuit breaker and degraded mode. If readiness depends on it, the load balancer loses every target even though search, caches and degraded answers still work.

check.q: A provider call has a 8 s timeout, two attempts, and the user-facing deadline is 15 s. What is wrong?
options: The worst case for the primary alone is about 16 s, so the deadline is exceeded and no time is left for a fallback
Nothing, retries are always good
Timeouts should always be longer than the deadline
Two attempts is too few for any provider
check.why: 8 + backoff + 8 is over 15 s. Timeouts along a path must sum below the deadline; shrink per-call timeouts and retry only when remaining budget allows.

check.q: Which error should NOT count toward opening a circuit breaker on a provider?
options: Timeout
HTTP 503
HTTP 429 rate limit
HTTP 400 invalid request caused by your own prompt format
check.why: A 400 means your request was invalid; the provider is healthy. Counting it would take a healthy provider out of rotation because of your bug. Timeouts, 429 and 5xx are retryable and count.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Containerization, CI/CD, logs, health checks, cost, latency and provider failures.
> **Prerequisites:** Python backend week.
> **Estimated time:** 50 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Deployment/runbook walkthrough.

## What LLMOps is

LLMOps is the practice of keeping an LLM-backed service **deployable, observable, affordable and survivable**. It is ordinary production engineering plus four new things: a dependency you do not control (the model provider), cost that scales with tokens, outputs that can be wrong without raising an error, and prompts and models that behave like code but are not in your type system. For system design and eval methodology see the **GenAI End to End course**; this lesson is about shipping and running the container.

You should always be able to answer five questions from a dashboard, not a guess: **Is it up? Is it fast enough? What does it cost? Is it good? What changed?** (code, prompt, model and index versions). If the last one has no answer, every incident takes hours.

## Containerizing a Python/FastAPI service

An image is a frozen filesystem plus a start command. The image that passed CI must be byte-for-byte the image that runs in production.

| Practice | Why | Breaks without it |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-stage build | Compilers and pip caches stay in the builder; runtime has only the venv and your code | 1 GB images, slow deploys, bigger attack surface |
| Slim base, pinned (digest if possible) | Predictable | A rebuild silently changes the OS layer |
| Pinned dependencies (lock file, hashes if possible) | An SDK minor bump can change retry or streaming behaviour | Yesterday's eval is no longer reproducible |
| Non-root user | A compromised process cannot modify system paths | Easier privilege escalation |
| Dependencies layer before code layer | Code edits reuse the cached install layer | Every commit reinstalls all packages |
| `.dockerignore` (`.git`, `.env`, `data/`) | Keeps secrets out of the build context | An API key baked into an image layer |
| Exec-form `CMD` | Server is PID 1 and gets SIGTERM, so it can drain requests | Deploys cut streams mid-answer |
| `HEALTHCHECK` | Orchestrator can restart a wedged process | A hung process keeps taking traffic |

With a hosted API there are no model weights in the image. If you self-host a small embedding model, keep weights on a mounted volume or artifact store and pin the version.

**Liveness vs readiness.** `/healthz` asks "is the process alive?" and makes no dependency calls; failure means restart. `/readyz` asks "should this instance receive traffic?" and checks cheap local dependencies (DB pool, Redis, index loaded); failure means stop routing, not restart. **Never make readiness call the LLM provider**: in a provider outage every instance goes not-ready together, the load balancer has zero targets, and a partial outage (search, cached answers, degraded mode still work) becomes a total one. Provider health belongs in the circuit breaker.

## Configuration and secrets

Config lives in the environment; the same image runs everywhere. Secrets come from the platform secret store or mounted files, never from the repo and never `ENV` in the Dockerfile (they persist in layers and show in `docker history`). Validate config at startup and **fail fast** if something is missing. Treat `PROMPT_VERSION` and `MODEL` as versioned config and put them in every log line and trace so you can correlate a quality or cost change with a deploy. Support two active keys during rotation.

## CI/CD with AI-specific gates

| Gate | Runs | Blocks when |
|---|---|---|
| Unit and contract tests with a **fake provider** | Every commit, no network, no cost | Parsing, retry, tool-schema or guardrail logic breaks |
| **Offline eval** on a golden set (30-200 cases) | PRs touching prompts, retrieval, models or tools | Pass rate or groundedness drops beyond a tolerance vs main |
| Image and dependency scan | Build | Critical findings |
| **Canary** (1-5% traffic) | After deploy | Error rate, p95, cost per request or a quality proxy regress |
| Automatic rollback | During canary | A hard SLO breach |

Evals are tests, but noisy and costly: gate on a threshold with tolerance, not equality, use a small golden set on PRs and a larger one nightly, and calibrate LLM judges against human labels. **A prompt change or a model change is a production deploy** and goes through the same gate and canary. Rollback means redeploying the previous version of everything that changed: image, prompt, model snapshot, index version. Pin the model to a dated snapshot when offered; a floating alias can change behaviour under you.

## Observability

**Logs.** One structured JSON line per request with a propagated `request_id`. Log metadata: tenant id, route, provider, model, prompt version, input and output tokens, per-stage latency, cache hit, retrieved doc ids and scores, tools called, finish reason, error class, retry count, guardrail verdict, cost estimate.

**Do not log by default:** raw prompts and answers, retrieved private chunks, API keys and auth headers, tool arguments with PII (emails, card numbers, addresses), anything under GDPR, HIPAA or PCI limits. If you need content to debug, sample a small percentage into a separate access-controlled store with short retention, redact first, and make it opt-in per tenant. Log lengths and hashes when you only need correlation.

**Traces.** A request becomes a tree of spans (see diagram). Put attributes on LLM spans in the style of the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (still evolving, check the current spec): provider, request model, input and output tokens, finish reason, plus your own `prompt.version`. That turns "the bot is slow" into "rerank p95 rose from 120 ms to 900 ms after Tuesday's deploy", and makes agent loops debuggable.

**Metrics.** Error rate by class (timeout, 429, 5xx, validation, guardrail); latency p50, p95, p99 per stage plus **time to first token**; tokens per request; **cost per request** and daily spend per tenant; cache hit rates; breaker state and fallback or degraded rate; ingestion queue depth and oldest-job age; quality proxies (thumbs down, human escalation, no-answer and missing-citation rates). Define SLOs, for example 99% of requests succeed (degraded counts) over 30 days and p95 time to first token under 2 s, and alert on error-budget **burn rate**, not every blip.

## Reliability: assume the provider is slow, wrong and sometimes gone

Apply in this order:

1. **Timeouts** everywhere: an overall deadline, a per-call timeout, and a stall timeout on streams. Without them one slow call holds a worker for minutes.
2. **Retries** with exponential backoff and jitter, only for retryable errors (timeout, 429, 5xx), honouring `Retry-After`, with a budget. Retrying 400s is a bug; retries without jitter synchronise into a herd; three attempts on every request triples load on a struggling provider.
3. **Circuit breaker**: after N consecutive failures skip the provider for a cool-down, then allow one probe (half-open). It converts a 20 s timeout per request into a 1 ms skip.
4. **Fallback provider or smaller model** with the same prompt contract, **tested by evals** because tool-call format, JSON mode and context size differ across providers.
5. **Graceful degradation** decided in advance: documents without a generated answer, cached answer, search-only mode, queue and notify, or an honest error. A write-capable agent should usually fail closed.
6. **Rate limits and budgets** per tenant and global, a concurrency semaphore around provider calls, and priority so batch jobs cannot starve interactive users. **Idempotency keys** for retried side effects.
7. **Queues for slow work**: ingestion (parse, chunk, embed) runs on workers with retries, a dead-letter queue and backpressure, never inside a web request.

**Worked example.** Provider p50 is 2 s, p99 is 12 s, user deadline is 15 s. Per-call timeout 8 s with two attempts gives 8 + 0.2 + 8 = 16.2 s for the primary alone: over budget, nothing left for the fallback. Fix: 5 s timeout, retry only when `deadline - elapsed > timeout`, then fall back with the remaining budget. **The timeouts along a path must sum to less than the deadline**, or they are decorative.

## Cost and latency

Cost per request = input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price, plus embedding, rerank and tool costs. Illustrative prices (made up; use your provider's page): 3 USD per million input tokens, 15 USD per million output tokens.

| Component | Tokens | Cost (USD) |
|---|---|---|
| System prompt and examples | 600 | 0.0018 |
| Retrieved context, 5 chunks x 400 | 2,000 | 0.0060 |
| History plus question | 400 | 0.0012 |
| **Input** | **3,000** | **0.0090** |
| **Output** | **400** | **0.0060** |
| **Total** | | **about 0.015** |

At 100,000 requests a day that is about 1,500 USD a day. Levers: fewer and better chunks via reranking, route easy queries to a smaller model, exact and semantic caching, provider prompt caching for the stable prefix (check docs for discounts and minimum sizes), `max_tokens` caps, history summarisation, batch APIs for offline work. **Agents multiply cost**: each step re-sends a growing context, so a six-step loop can cost around 10x one call.

Latency of a RAG answer is roughly embed query (50-150 ms) + search (20-100 ms) + rerank (100-400 ms) + time to first token (300-1500 ms) + output tokens divided by tokens per second. 400 tokens at about 50 tokens/s is 8 s, so **streaming** is the biggest perceived win. These are order-of-magnitude figures; measure your own.

**Cutting p95 without hurting quality:** trace per stage first, since tails come from specific stages. Then, lowest risk first: parallelise independent stages, stream, cap output length, trim context rather than model quality, cache embeddings and answers, hedge slow calls (second request after the p95 delay, cancel the loser, costs extra), route simple queries to a faster model, move logging and suggestions off the critical path. Prove quality held with the offline eval.

## Common failure modes

Token growth doubling the bill after a prompt or retrieval change (no cost-per-version metric); retry storms in a provider incident; readiness probes calling the provider; raw prompts in general-access logs; floating model aliases; a fallback provider never exercised until the outage; unbounded agent loops or concurrency; an ingestion backlog that makes answers stale with no alert.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The container ran as root, baked an API key into the image, and had no health check, so the load balancer kept sending traffic to a process that was hung on the provider. CI deployed on green unit tests that never called the model. Logs were `print`. Cost doubled overnight because a retry loop had no cap and the cache key included a timestamp. The runbook was 'restart the pod'.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'p95 latency jumped from 1.2 s to 8 s. Where do you look?' Outline: provider time-to-first-token vs your queue, cache hit rate, batch size, and whether a release changed the prompt. Follow-up: 'How do you roll back?' Answer: previous image tag, a feature flag on the new prompt, and a health check that fails if error rate or TTFT crosses a line.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a Kubernetes-from-scratch week unless the JD asks. Keep a Dockerfile, one pipeline, health, structured logs, a cost cap, and a rollback you can name.

parts.label: Worked example
parts.body:
## Goal and artifact

Produce a **deployment and runbook walkthrough** you can present in 10 minutes: a container that builds, runs locally with `docker compose up`, exposes liveness and readiness endpoints, logs structured metadata without content, survives a simulated provider outage through a circuit breaker and fallback, and has a runbook an on-call engineer could follow at 3 a.m.

## What each file is and what it proves

| File | Purpose | What proves it works |
|---|---|---|
| `Dockerfile` | Multi-stage, pinned, non-root, healthcheck, exec-form CMD | `docker build`, then `docker run --rm app id` prints a non-root uid; `docker image ls` shows a small runtime image |
| `requirements.txt` | Exact pins (the versions shown are illustrative; generate your own with pip-compile or uv) | Two builds a week apart give the same installed set |
| `compose.yaml` | API, ingestion worker, Postgres with pgvector, Redis; healthcheck-gated start order; secrets as files; read-only root filesystem and resource limits | `docker compose up` starts in order; `docker compose ps` shows healthy |
| `app/main.py` | `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/chat`; JSON logs with metadata only | Log line contains tokens, latency, provider, request id, but no question text |
| `app/resilience.py` | Circuit breaker plus fallback client with a degraded mode | The tests below |
| `tests/test_resilience.py` | Fake clock and fake providers; no network | `python -m unittest` passes in under a second |

Run the tests from the project root with `python -m unittest tests.test_resilience` (put an empty `app/__init__.py` and `tests/__init__.py` in place).

## Design decisions to be able to defend

- **The breaker counts only retryable errors.** A 400 from the provider means your request was invalid; tripping the breaker on it would take a healthy provider out of rotation because of your bug. The test `test_non_retryable_error_does_not_trip_breaker_or_fallback` pins this.
- **Half-open lets exactly one probe through.** Otherwise the moment the cool-down ends, hundreds of queued requests hit a recovering provider and knock it over again.
- **Clock and sleep are injected.** That is what lets the tests run instantly and deterministically. Any time-dependent logic should take its clock as a parameter.
- **Degraded mode is explicit in the response** (`degraded: true`) so the UI can say "limited mode" and your metrics can count it. Silent degradation is how quality regressions hide.
- **Logs carry `question_chars`, not the question.** Enough to spot a prompt-length regression, nothing sensitive.
- **Production extras not shown, and you should say so:** jitter on backoff, a per-request deadline that shrinks the per-call timeout, a concurrency semaphore, a real DB and Redis check in `/readyz`, and exporting breaker state as a metric.

## Adding a trace span (OpenTelemetry style)

Wrap the provider call so the span carries model and token counts. The attribute names follow the GenAI semantic conventions at the time of writing; check the current spec because they have been renamed before.

```python
from opentelemetry import trace

tracer = trace.get_tracer("assistant")

def traced_call(provider_name: str, model: str, call, prompt: str, timeout: float):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("llm.call") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", model)
        span.set_attribute("llm.provider", provider_name)
        span.set_attribute("prompt.version", "support-v7")
        text, tokens_in, tokens_out = call(prompt, timeout)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", tokens_in)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", tokens_out)
        return text, tokens_in, tokens_out
```

Exceptions raised inside the `with` block are recorded on the span by the OpenTelemetry SDK by default, which is what you want for provider errors.

## Runbook template

Copy this for each alert. A good runbook is short, starts with symptoms and ends with who to call.

```text
RUNBOOK: LLM provider slow or failing
Owner: <team> | Last reviewed: <date> | Alert: llm_error_rate_burn_fast

1. SYMPTOMS
   - p95 chat latency > 8 s for 5 min, or error rate > 5 percent
   - breaker_state{provider="primary"} = open, fallback_rate rising
   - Users report: slow answers, "limited mode" banner

2. DASHBOARDS (open in this order)
   - Service overview: requests, error rate by class, p50/p95/p99
   - LLM stages: time to first token, tokens per request, cost per request
   - Provider status page and our breaker/fallback panel
   - Recent deploys: image, prompt version, model version, index version

3. TRIAGE QUESTIONS
   a. Did we deploy in the last 60 minutes? (yes -> step 4A)
   b. Is the error class 429? (yes -> we are over quota or a tenant is flooding -> 4B)
   c. Is it 5xx or timeouts across all tenants? (yes -> provider incident -> 4C)
   d. Is token count per request up? (yes -> prompt/retrieval regression -> 4A)

4. MITIGATIONS (least to most disruptive)
   A. Roll back the last change: image, prompt version and model alias together.
   B. Lower the offending tenant's rate limit; confirm the global concurrency cap.
   C. Force traffic to the fallback provider (flag LLM_PRIMARY_DISABLED=true).
      If both are down: enable degraded mode (retrieval-only answers).
   D. Pause ingestion workers if they compete for quota; the queue will catch up.
   E. Raise the status banner. Do not disable the daily budget cap.

5. VERIFY
   - Error rate and p95 back under SLO for 15 min; breaker closed; fallback rate near zero.

6. AFTER
   - Timeline in the incident doc; was detection fast enough? Add or tune an alert.
   - Add the failing case to the eval set or the chaos test.

7. ESCALATE to <role> if: no improvement after 30 min, data exposure suspected, or spend > 2x daily budget.
```

## Chaos drill (30 minutes)

Make `primary` raise `RetryableError` via an environment flag, send 20 requests, and confirm: responses still arrive from `secondary`, the logs show `provider=secondary`, and after you remove the flag and wait out the cool-down the breaker returns to closed. Then make both fail and confirm `degraded: true` responses. Record before and after numbers as **illustrative measurements from your machine**, not benchmarks.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The container ran as root, baked an API key into the image, and had no health check, so the load balancer kept sending traffic to a process that was hung on the provider. CI deployed on green unit tests that never called the model. Logs were `print`. Cost doubled overnight because a retry loop had no cap and the cache key included a timestamp. The runbook was 'restart the pod'.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'p95 latency jumped from 1.2 s to 8 s. Where do you look?' Outline: provider time-to-first-token vs your queue, cache hit rate, batch size, and whether a release changed the prompt. Follow-up: 'How do you roll back?' Answer: previous image tag, a feature flag on the new prompt, and a health check that fails if error rate or TTFT crosses a line.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut a Kubernetes-from-scratch week unless the JD asks. Keep a Dockerfile, one pipeline, health, structured logs, a cost cap, and a rollback you can name.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# ---- build stage: compilers and pip live here, never in the final image ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
ENV PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1
WORKDIR /build
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
# requirements.txt is generated by pip-compile or uv with exact pins (and hashes if you can)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

# ---- runtime stage: only the venv and your code ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
# non-root user with no shell login and no home directory
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --gid app --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app
WORKDIR /srv
COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY --chown=app:app app ./app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
# liveness only: the process answers. Dependencies are checked by /readyz, not here.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"
# exec form so uvicorn is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--timeout-graceful-shutdown", "20"]

# docker-compose.yaml: local stack that mirrors production topology
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    env_file: .env            # LLM_API_KEY, DATABASE_URL ... never committed, never baked into the image
    environment:
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
      LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "20"
      LOG_LEVEL: info
    depends_on:
      db:    { condition: service_healthy }
      cache: { condition: service_healthy }
    restart: unless-stopped
    read_only: true            # container filesystem is immutable
    tmpfs: ["/tmp"]
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M }

  worker:                      # ingestion: same image, different command, no public port
    build: .
    command: ["python", "-m", "app.worker"]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
    depends_on:
      db:    { condition: service_healthy }
      cache: { condition: service_healthy }
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    secrets: [db_password]
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt   # git-ignored

volumes:
  pgdata:

import unittest

from app.resilience import (AllProvidersFailed, CircuitBreaker, FallbackClient,
                            Provider, ProviderError, RetryableError)


class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.now = 0.0

    def __call__(self):
        return self.now


def ok(name):
    return lambda prompt, timeout: (f"{name}:{prompt}", 10, 5)


def always_fail(prompt, timeout):
    raise RetryableError("503")


class BreakerTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_opens_after_threshold_and_recovers_via_probe(self):
        clock = FakeClock()
        b = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, reset_after=30, clock=clock)
        for _ in range(3):
            self.assertTrue(b.allow())
            b.record_failure()
        self.assertEqual(b.state, "open")
        self.assertFalse(b.allow())
        clock.now = 31
        self.assertEqual(b.state, "half_open")
        self.assertTrue(b.allow())       # the single probe
        self.assertFalse(b.allow())      # a second concurrent call is refused
        b.record_success()
        self.assertEqual(b.state, "closed")

    def test_failed_probe_reopens(self):
        clock = FakeClock()
        b = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=1, reset_after=10, clock=clock)
        b.record_failure()
        clock.now = 11
        self.assertTrue(b.allow())
        b.record_failure()
        self.assertEqual(b.state, "open")
        clock.now = 15
        self.assertEqual(b.state, "open")  # cool-down restarted at t=11


class FallbackTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def make(self, primary_call, degraded=None):
        clock = FakeClock()
        sleeps = []
        primary = Provider("primary", primary_call, CircuitBreaker(2, 30, clock))
        secondary = Provider("secondary", ok("secondary"), CircuitBreaker(2, 30, clock))
        client = FallbackClient([primary, secondary], degraded=degraded,
                                max_attempts=2, backoff=0.1, sleep=sleeps.append)
        return client, primary, sleeps

    def test_uses_primary_when_healthy(self):
        client, _, _ = self.make(ok("primary"))
        self.assertEqual(client.complete("hi").provider, "primary")

    def test_retries_with_backoff_then_falls_back(self):
        client, primary, sleeps = self.make(always_fail)
        result = client.complete("hi")
        self.assertEqual(result.provider, "secondary")
        self.assertEqual(sleeps, [0.1])          # one backoff between two attempts
        self.assertEqual(primary.breaker.state, "open")  # two failures reached the threshold

    def test_open_circuit_skips_primary_without_calling_it(self):
        calls = []

        def counting(prompt, timeout):
            calls.append(1)
            raise RetryableError("503")

        client, _, _ = self.make(counting)
        client.complete("a")
        before = len(calls)
        client.complete("b")
        self.assertEqual(len(calls), before)     # circuit open: primary not touched

    def test_non_retryable_error_does_not_trip_breaker_or_fallback(self):
        def bad_request(prompt, timeout):
            raise ProviderError("400 invalid request")

        client, primary, _ = self.make(bad_request)
        with self.assertRaises(ProviderError):
            client.complete("hi")
        self.assertEqual(primary.breaker.state, "closed")

    def test_degraded_answer_when_everything_is_down(self):
        down = Provider("only", always_fail, CircuitBreaker(1, 30, FakeClock()))
        client = FallbackClient([down], degraded=lambda p: "limited mode", sleep=lambda s: None)
        result = client.complete("hi")
        self.assertTrue(result.degraded)
        self.assertEqual(result.text, "limited mode")

    def test_raises_when_no_degraded_mode(self):
        down = Provider("only", always_fail, CircuitBreaker(1, 30, FakeClock()))
        client = FallbackClient([down], sleep=lambda s: None)
        with self.assertRaises(AllProvidersFailed):
            client.complete("hi")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
How to use this: say the 60-90 second version out loud, then check the structured answer. If you have not run these things in production, say so plainly and describe what you built locally (the worked example) and how you would validate the rest.

## Q1. What should you log and trace, and what sensitive data should not be logged?

**Define.** Logs record discrete events with metadata; traces record the timed tree of steps in one request; together they let you reconstruct what happened without storing what users said.

**Mechanism.** One structured JSON line per request with a request id that is propagated to every stage. Log provider, model, prompt version, token counts, per-stage latency, cache hits, retrieved document ids and scores, tool names, finish reason, error class, retries, guardrail verdicts and a cost estimate. Trace each stage as a span (retrieve, rerank, `llm.call`, tool calls) with token counts as attributes, so a slow request shows which stage ate the time.

**Decision.** Never log by default: raw prompts and completions, retrieved private chunks, secrets and auth headers, PII in tool arguments, anything under GDPR, HIPAA or PCI constraints. If content is needed for debugging or evals, sample a small fraction into a separate store with strict access, short retention and redaction, opt-in per tenant. For correlation use lengths, hashes and ids.

**Trade-off.** Less content in logs means slower debugging of individual bad answers. You pay that with good retrieval-id logging (you can re-fetch the chunk from the source of truth), replayable test cases, and user feedback that explicitly attaches a conversation for review.

**Evidence.** In the worked example the log line carries `question_chars` and tokens but no text. If you have not run it in production, say so and describe the test: grep the logs for a canary string you sent in the question and confirm it is absent.

**Failure mode to mention.** Debug-level logging turned on during an incident quietly writes full prompts to a log system many people can read.

**60-90 second version:** "I log metadata, not content: request id, model and prompt version, token counts, stage latencies, cache hit, retrieved document ids, tool names, finish reason, error class and a cost estimate, as one JSON line per request. I trace each stage as a span so I can see whether retrieval, rerank or the LLM call caused a slow request. I do not log raw prompts or answers, retrieved private text, keys, or PII in tool arguments. If I need content for debugging, I sample into a separate access-controlled store with redaction and short retention. The trade-off is slower debugging, which I offset with logging document ids so I can re-fetch evidence."

**Follow-ups.**
- *How do you debug one bad answer, then?* Look up the request id, see prompt version and retrieved ids, re-run the same inputs from the source documents in a staging environment, add it to the eval set.
- *Where do the token counts come from?* From the provider's usage field in the response; estimate with a tokenizer only when streaming does not return usage.
- *What about user consent?* Content sampling is opt-in per tenant and covered in the data processing terms.

## Q2. How would the product behave if the model provider is slow or unavailable?

**Define.** Graceful degradation: the product keeps delivering reduced but honest value, and fails closed where an action would be unsafe.

**Mechanism.** Deadlines and timeouts bound the damage of a slow call. Retries with backoff and jitter handle transient errors. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing provider and probes for recovery. A fallback chain routes to a second provider or smaller model. If nothing is available, degraded mode returns retrieval results without a generated answer, a cached answer, or a queued request with a notification. The response says it is degraded.

**Decision.** Per feature: a read-only Q&A feature degrades to search results; a refund-issuing agent fails closed and tells the user a human will follow up; batch summarisation just queues and retries later. Do not make readiness probes depend on the provider.

**Trade-off.** Fallback providers cost integration and eval effort and are not perfectly compatible (JSON mode, tool-call format, context size); degraded answers are lower value; retries add load and latency. Keep retry budgets small and make the sum of timeouts fit the deadline.

**Evidence.** Describe the chaos drill: force the primary to return retryable errors, show traffic moving to the secondary, the breaker opening and closing, and degraded responses when both are down. If you only ran it locally, say that, and say you would repeat it in staging with real provider errors.

**Failure mode to mention.** A retry storm: no jitter, three attempts per request, and the provider's recovery is pushed back by your own traffic. A related one: a fallback never exercised until the outage turns out to be incompatible.

**60-90 second version:** "I assume the provider will be slow and sometimes down. Every call has a timeout inside an overall deadline, and retries are limited, jittered and only for retryable errors. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing provider after consecutive failures and sends one probe after a cool-down. Traffic falls back to a second provider that I have tested with the same eval set. If everything is down, the feature degrades: Q&A returns the relevant documents with a banner, and anything with side effects fails closed. I'd monitor breaker state, fallback rate and degraded rate and alert on burn of the error budget."

**Follow-ups.**
- *Why not retry forever?* It multiplies load during an outage and violates the user's deadline.
- *How do you pick breaker thresholds?* From observed error rates and traffic; for example five consecutive failures or a failure rate above 50% over a window with a minimum request count, then tune from incident reviews.
- *What if the fallback is worse?* Accept it for availability, mark it, and keep the eval number for the fallback so you know the cost.

## Q3. How would you reduce p95 latency without damaging answer quality?

**Define.** p95 is the latency under which 95% of requests complete; the goal is to shrink the slow tail while holding eval scores constant.

**Mechanism.** Measure first: per-stage traces show where tails come from (often rerank, a cold cache, long outputs, or a retry). Then change the cheapest, safest things first: stream output so time to first token is what users feel; parallelise independent steps; cap output length and request concise formats; shrink context with better retrieval and reranking instead of a weaker model; cache embeddings and frequent answers; hedge slow calls; route easy queries to a faster model; move analytics off the critical path.

**Decision.** Attack the largest stage at p95, not the mean. Swapping to a smaller model is the riskiest lever, so do it behind routing with an eval gate.

**Trade-off.** Hedging costs extra tokens; caching risks stale answers (set TTLs and invalidate on document updates); shorter outputs can lose detail; routing adds a classifier that can mis-route.

**Evidence.** Before and after numbers from your own traces (labelled illustrative) plus the eval pass rate unchanged within tolerance. If you have not tuned a live system, say you would build the per-stage latency dashboard first.

**Failure mode to mention.** Optimising the average while p99 is dominated by retries; or trimming context so aggressively that groundedness drops, which the latency dashboard will not show.

**60-90 second version:** "First I'd get per-stage p95 from traces, because the tail usually comes from one stage. Then I'd work from low risk to high: stream so users see text in about a second, parallelise independent retrieval steps, cap output length, cut context through better retrieval and reranking, cache embeddings and repeat questions, and hedge slow calls. Model routing to a smaller model is the riskiest, so it goes behind the offline eval gate and a canary. Every change must keep the golden-set score within tolerance; otherwise it's not a latency win, it's a quality regression."

**Follow-ups.**
- *Is streaming real latency reduction?* No, total time is unchanged; it reduces perceived latency. Still the biggest UX win.
- *How do you cache LLM answers safely?* Key on normalised question plus tenant plus document version, short TTL, invalidate on re-index, never share across tenants.
- *Where could quality drop unnoticed?* Truncated context and shorter outputs; track groundedness and answer completeness online.

## Q4. Estimate per-request cost and explain which inputs drive the estimate.

**Define.** Cost per request is the sum of token charges (input and output) plus retrieval, embedding, rerank and infrastructure costs, multiplied by calls per request.

**Mechanism.** Count tokens by component: system prompt, retrieved context, history, question, output. Multiply input tokens by the input price and output tokens by the output price. Using the illustrative prices of 3 and 15 USD per million tokens: 3,000 input tokens cost 0.009 USD, 400 output tokens cost 0.006 USD, total about 0.015 USD. At 100,000 requests a day, about 1,500 USD. Multiply by the number of LLM calls for agent loops, and subtract cache hits: with a 30% hit rate, the model cost is about 0.7 x 1,500 = 1,050 USD.

**Decision.** The drivers, ranked: context size (chunks x chunk size), output length, number of calls per request, model tier, cache hit rate, retries. Optimise the largest term first.

**Trade-off.** Cheaper means smaller context, smaller model or more caching, each with a quality or freshness risk, so tie each lever to the eval.

**Evidence.** Compare your estimate against logged token counts and the provider's usage report for a week; the gap reveals hidden calls (retries, judge calls, tool loops). If you only have an estimate, say so and name the assumptions.

**Failure mode to mention.** Forgetting that retries, guardrail or judge calls and multi-step agents multiply the number of billed calls; also that input price differs from output price and cached-input price.

**60-90 second version:** "I break a request into tokens by component: about 600 system prompt, 2,000 retrieved context, 400 history and question, 400 output. With illustrative prices of 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output, that's 0.009 plus 0.006, about 1.5 cents per request, 1,500 dollars a day at 100k requests. The drivers are context size, output length, calls per request and model tier; caching and routing change the multiplier. I'd validate against actual usage logs, because retries and judge calls hide extra spend."

**Follow-ups.**
- *How would you cap spend?* Per-tenant daily budget, max output tokens, step limit for agents, and an alert at 80%.
- *Does prompt caching change the estimate?* It discounts the repeated prefix on supported providers; check current docs for rates and minimum prefix size.
- *Self-hosting to save money?* Only past enough steady utilisation to cover GPUs, ops and idle time; compute break-even before moving.

## Q5 (added). How do you ship a prompt or model change safely?

**Define.** Treat it as a deploy: versioned, evaluated, canaried and reversible.

**Mechanism.** Prompt stored in the repo with a version id; PR runs unit tests and the golden-set eval; merge triggers a canary at 1-5% with comparison on error rate, p95, cost and quality proxies; automatic rollback on breach. The prompt version is in every log and trace.

**Decision.** Use shadow mode (run new, serve old) when quality risk is high. **Trade-off:** eval cost and slower iteration versus silent regressions. **Evidence:** a table of eval scores for old and new, and the canary dashboard. **Failure mode to mention:** a floating model alias changing behaviour with no deploy on your side.

**60-90 second version:** "A prompt change is a code change. It has a version id, runs through the golden-set eval in CI, then a small canary with automatic rollback if error rate, p95, cost or a quality proxy regresses. I pin the model snapshot so behaviour only changes when I change it."

**Follow-ups.** *What if eval and online disagree?* Trust online, then add the failing cases to the eval. *Who approves?* Same code review path as code.

## Q6 (added). Walk me through your Dockerfile for an AI service.

**Define.** A reproducible, minimal, least-privilege image. **Mechanism.** Multi-stage build so build tools stay out; pinned base and dependencies; dependencies layer before code for cache reuse; non-root user; `.dockerignore`; exec-form CMD so SIGTERM reaches the server; a healthcheck that tests liveness only. **Decision:** keep secrets and model weights out of the image. **Trade-off:** slim images lack debugging tools, so use ephemeral debug containers. **Evidence:** show `docker history` has no secrets and the container runs as a non-root uid. **Failure mode to mention:** an `.env` copied into a layer.

**60-90 second version:** "Two stages: the builder installs pinned dependencies into a virtualenv, the runtime copies only the venv and the app, runs as a non-root user, starts uvicorn in exec form so it handles SIGTERM, and has a liveness healthcheck. Secrets come from the environment at runtime, never baked in."

**Follow-ups.** *Liveness vs readiness?* Restart versus route. *Why pin by digest?* Tags are mutable.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. The container ran as root, baked an API key into the image, and had no health check, so the load balancer kept sending traffic to a process that was hung on the provider. CI deployed on green unit tests that never called the model. Logs were `print`. Cost doubled overnight because a retry loop had no cap and the cache key included a timestamp. The runbook was 'restart the pod'.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'p95 latency jumped from 1.2 s to 8 s. Where do you look?' Outline: provider time-to-first-token vs your queue, cache hit rate, batch size, and whether a release changed the prompt. Follow-up: 'How do you roll back?' Answer: previous image tag, a feature flag on the new prompt, and a health check that fails if error rate or TTFT crosses a line.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut a Kubernetes-from-scratch week unless the JD asks. Keep a Dockerfile, one pipeline, health, structured logs, a cost cap, and a rollback you can name.

lessons.title: AWS and Redis for AI services: deploy a RAG API
lessons.summary: A practical AWS reference deployment for a FastAPI RAG or agent API, with Redis for caching, rate limits and idempotency, tested offline code and a least-privilege IAM policy.
keyPoints: Reference stack: S3 for documents, SQS plus dead-letter queue for ingestion, Fargate for API and workers, Postgres with pgvector, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch.
Fargate suits streaming, long-lived LLM APIs and minutes-long workers; Lambda suits small spiky glue but has time limits and per-instance connection pools.
Put tenant, generation counter, access scope and a payload hash in every cache key; bump the generation to invalidate and never share permission-scoped answers.
Rate limit with an atomic token bucket (Lua, Redis TIME), charged by tokens; use SET NX idempotency keys for side-effecting retries.
Locks give efficiency, not correctness; keep durable keys away from evicting cache instances.
Redis is an optimisation: short timeouts, caught errors and per-route fail-open or fail-closed rules keep the app up when it is down.
Task role gets specific actions on specific ARNs; separate it from the ECS execution role. Check current docs for quotas and ARN forms.

check.q: A user's group membership changes and they must lose access to cached answers now. What is the safest cache design?
options: Rely on a 1 hour TTL
Put the access scope in the key, authorise before every cache read, and bump the generation for urgent revocation
Cache by question hash only and filter results in the browser
Flush the whole Redis instance each night
check.why: Scope in the key stops cross-user hits, authorising first stops revoked users reading, and a generation bump makes old entries unreachable immediately. TTL alone leaves a stale window.

check.q: Why run a token-bucket rate limiter as a single Lua script in Redis?
options: Lua is faster than any client language
It lets Redis store more data
Redis cannot run INCR without Lua
The read-modify-write executes atomically, so concurrent requests cannot both spend the last token
check.why: Doing GET, compute, SET from the client allows interleaving between containers. A script runs without other commands interleaved, and TIME avoids clock skew.

check.q: Which choice best fits a streaming chat API whose model calls take 5 to 30 seconds and use a Postgres pool?
options: Lambda behind API Gateway with one connection per invocation
ECS on Fargate behind an ALB
A single EC2 instance with a cron job
Redis Streams as the request transport
check.why: Fargate runs long-lived processes with no per-request time limit, handles streaming naturally and keeps database pools healthy. Lambda is better for small event glue.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** A practical AWS reference deployment for a FastAPI RAG or agent API, with Redis for caching, rate limits and idempotency, tested offline code and a least-privilege IAM policy.
> **Prerequisites:** Docker, cloud and LLMOps week.
> **Estimated time:** 45 min reading, then the hands-on task. Apply it once in your next weekly review or mock, using the lesson's worked example or template.

## What you are building and why this lesson exists

A RAG or agent API is a normal web service with three unusual properties: its main dependency (the model provider) is slow, metered and rate-limited; its data (documents, embeddings) is large, per-tenant and changes; and its answers can leak data if you cache them carelessly. AWS gives you the boring infrastructure (storage, queues, compute, identity, logs). Redis gives you a fast shared memory in front of the expensive parts. This lesson is the **practical** level: enough to draw the architecture, write the runbook and defend each choice. It is not a certification dive.

You already know Docker and FastAPI. Here the container is the unit you hand to AWS.

## Reference deployment

```text
client -> ALB (or API Gateway) -> ECS Fargate service "api" (FastAPI)
                                      |-> Redis (cache, limits, idempotency)
                                      |-> Postgres + pgvector (RDS / Aurora)
                                      |-> Bedrock or provider API (via NAT / VPC endpoint)
S3 (documents) -> event -> SQS "ingest" -> ECS Fargate service "worker"
                                             |-> chunk, embed, upsert to Postgres, bump cache generation
```

| Piece | Job | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| **S3** | Source documents, parsed text, exports | Cheap, durable, event notifications, per-prefix IAM |
| **SQS** | Ingestion queue plus a dead-letter queue | Decouples upload from slow embedding; retries and visibility timeout built in |
| **ECS on Fargate** | Runs the API and the workers as containers | No servers to patch; long-lived processes and streaming responses work |
| **Lambda** (alternative) | Same code per request or per SQS batch | Scale to zero, pay per use, but time limit and cold starts |
| **ALB or API Gateway** | Front door, TLS, health checks | ALB for a container service; API Gateway when you want API keys, usage plans, per-route throttling |
| **RDS or Aurora Postgres + pgvector** | Metadata, chunks, vectors, jobs | One database you already know; vector search next to relational filters |
| **Secrets Manager / Parameter Store** | Provider keys, DB passwords, config | Rotation and audit; Parameter Store is fine for non-secret config |
| **IAM task role** | Permissions of the running code | Least privilege, no long-lived keys in the image |
| **CloudWatch** | Logs, metrics, alarms | Default sink for ECS, Lambda and ALB |
| **VPC** | Network boundary | Private subnets for tasks, DB and Redis; public only for the load balancer |

### Fargate vs Lambda for the API

| Question | Fargate | Lambda |
|---|---|---|
| Cold start | None once tasks are running; a new task takes tens of seconds to start | Per-instance cold start; noticeable with big dependencies |
| Time limit | None per request | Hard maximum per invocation (check current docs); API Gateway also has its own integration timeout |
| Streaming tokens (SSE) | Natural | Possible with response streaming, but more setup |
| Idle cost | You pay for the running minimum tasks | Near zero |
| Connection pools (Postgres, Redis) | Long-lived pool per task | Each concurrent instance opens its own; need a proxy or small pools |
| Burst scaling | Minutes (autoscaling on CPU, requests or queue depth) | Fast, subject to account concurrency limits |
| Ops surface | Cluster, service, task definition | Function, layers or container image |

**Default answer:** Fargate for the streaming API and for workers that embed documents for minutes; Lambda for small spiky glue (an S3 event that enqueues a job, a webhook, a nightly cleanup). Say the reason out loud: LLM calls take seconds, streaming is the product experience, and database pools fit a long-lived process.

### Bedrock vs calling a provider API

| | Bedrock | Provider API directly |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | IAM role, no key to store | API key in Secrets Manager |
| Data path | Stays inside AWS; fits existing compliance and billing | Leaves to a third party |
| Models | Catalogue per region, may lag the newest release | Newest features first |
| Limits | Per-account, per-region quotas on requests and tokens | Per-key tier limits |
| Portability | Different request shapes per model family | Provider-specific too |

Quotas and prices change. **Check current docs** for model availability, tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute, and request increases before launch day, not on launch day.

### Cost levers (ordered by how often they matter)

1. **Do not call the model**: exact-match cache, embedding cache, refusing empty or duplicate requests.
2. **Smaller model for routine steps** (classification, rewriting), larger only for the final answer.
3. **Shorter prompts**: fewer retrieved chunks, trimmed history.
4. **Fargate right-sizing**: small CPU and memory per task, scale on queue depth for workers, Spot capacity for interruptible workers.
5. **NAT gateway traffic**: it is billed per hour and per GB; use VPC endpoints for S3 and other AWS services (gateway endpoint for S3).
6. **Log volume**: never log full prompts by default; set retention on log groups.

## Redis for AI services

Redis is an in-memory data store with a few useful structures: strings with TTL, counters, hashes, sorted sets, streams, and atomic Lua scripts. In an AI service it sits **in front of the model provider** and answers three questions cheaply: have I computed this already, may this caller proceed, and have I handled this request before.

### 1. Exact-match response cache

Key = hash of everything that can change the answer: tenant, model name, prompt version, normalised question, retrieved document ids and the user's access scope. Value = the validated answer. TTL bounds staleness.

*Worked number (illustrative):* an internal help bot gets 10,000 questions a day and 30% are repeats after normalisation. At a hypothetical 2 cents per answer, caching saves 3,000 x 0.02 = 60 dollars a day and removes 3,000 multi-second waits. Measure your own hit rate before you promise anything.

### 2. Embedding cache

Embedding the same text twice is waste. Key by `sha256(model + text)`; value is the vector. Safe to cache for a long time because the input fully determines the output. Invalidate only when you change the embedding model (put the model name in the key).

### 3. Semantic cache caveats

A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new question is *near* an old one in embedding space. The failure mode is a confident wrong answer: "How do I reset my password?" and "How do I reset my colleague's password?" are close vectors with different correct answers. If you use it: high similarity threshold, per-tenant and per-scope namespaces, only for low-stakes FAQ-style questions, and evaluate false-hit rate on a labelled set. Exact-match first; semantic only if the measured hit rate justifies the risk.

### 4. Rate limiting

Two algorithms to explain:

- **Fixed window via INCR + EXPIRE**: `INCR rl:tenant:minute` and set `EXPIRE` when the result is 1. Simple, but allows a burst of 2x at a window boundary. The INCR and EXPIRE are two commands; if the process dies between them the key never expires, so use a Lua script or `SET key 0 EX 60 NX` then `INCR`.
- **Token bucket**: capacity `C`, refill rate `r` per second, each request costs tokens. Allows bursts up to `C`, then sustained rate `r`. State is two numbers (tokens, last timestamp). Read-modify-write must be **atomic**, so run it as one Lua script (Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands) and take the clock from Redis `TIME`, not from the client.
- **Sliding window log** (sorted set of timestamps) is exact but costs memory per request.

For LLM apps rate-limit by **tokens or cost**, not only by request count: one long-context request can cost 100 short ones. Deduct an estimate up front and settle after the response.

### 5. Idempotency keys

Clients retry. A retried "create report" or "send email" tool call must not run twice. The client sends `Idempotency-Key`. The server does `SET key pending NX EX 120`; if that succeeds it runs the work, then stores the result under the key for 24 hours. A second request with the same key and same body returns the stored result; with a different body it is an error; while the first is running it gets "in progress". Store a hash of the body with the key.

### 6. Distributed locks and their pitfalls

`SET lock token NX PX 30000` gives you a lock with an expiry; release only if the stored token is yours (compare-and-delete in Lua). Pitfalls:

- The work outlives the TTL, so two holders run at once. A lock gives **efficiency** (avoid duplicate work), not **correctness**. If correctness matters, use a database constraint or a fencing token.
- Redis failover can lose the lock (replication is asynchronous).
- Releasing someone else's lock when you skip the token check.
- Prefer single-flight inside one process, and for cross-process work prefer an idempotency key or a Postgres unique constraint.

### 7. Queues and streams vs SQS

| | SQS | Redis Streams |
|---|---|---|
| Durability | Managed, replicated | Depends on persistence and replication settings |
| Retries and DLQ | Built in (visibility timeout, redrive) | You build consumer groups, pending-entry reclaim and dead-lettering |
| Ops | None | You run or pay for Redis |
| Latency | Tens of ms | Sub-millisecond |
| Replay | No | Yes, streams are logs |

**Default:** ingestion jobs go through SQS. Use Redis for ephemeral coordination, not as the system of record for work.

### 8. TTL and eviction

Every cache key needs a TTL. Eviction policy decides what happens when memory is full: `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu` suits a pure cache; `volatile-*` policies evict only keys with a TTL; `noeviction` makes writes fail, which suits idempotency data you must not lose. **Do not mix** durable keys (idempotency, locks) and evictable cache in one instance with `allkeys-lru`, or an eviction can silently delete an idempotency record. Two instances, or `volatile-lru` with TTLs on cache keys only.

### 9. Invalidation and permissions

- **Document changes:** keep a per-tenant (or per-collection) **generation number** in Redis and put it in every cache key. Updating a document does `INCR gen`, and all older keys become unreachable and age out. Cheaper and safer than scanning and deleting keys.
- **Permission changes:** the key must contain the caller's **access scope** (user id, or a hash of their group set). Never serve an answer computed under one user's permissions to another. When someone's groups change, their scope hash changes and old entries are simply never hit; also bump the generation for revoked access if you must stop cached reads immediately.
- **Per-tenant namespacing:** every key starts with `app:{tenant}:`. It prevents cross-tenant leaks and lets you delete or measure one tenant.

### 10. Persistence and failure behaviour

Redis can persist (RDB snapshots, AOF log) and replicate, but treat it as a **cache that may vanish**. The app must keep working when Redis is down or empty:

| Feature | Redis down behaviour |
|---|---|
| Response and embedding cache | Skip it, compute live (slower, costlier) |
| Rate limiter | Fail **open** for ordinary users plus a coarse in-process limit, or fail **closed** for expensive endpoints; decide per route |
| Idempotency | Fail closed for side-effecting actions (return 503) or fall back to a Postgres unique key |
| Locks | Fall back to in-process single-flight |

Always set short connection and command timeouts (tens to hundreds of milliseconds) so a dead Redis does not stall every request; add a circuit breaker so you stop trying for a few seconds after repeated errors.

## IAM, secrets, observability, network (the parts people skip)

- **Two roles on ECS:** the *execution role* lets ECS pull the image, write logs and fetch startup secrets; the *task role* is what your code uses. Keep the task role tiny. See the policy sketch in the worked example.
- **Secrets:** inject from Secrets Manager into the task as environment variables or fetch at startup. Never bake keys into the image or log them.
- **CloudWatch:** structured JSON logs (request id, tenant id, model, token counts, latency, cache hit), metrics for p95 latency, 5xx rate, queue age, DLQ depth, cache hit rate, rate-limit rejections, provider errors. Alarm on DLQ depth above zero, oldest message age, 5xx rate and a spend proxy (tokens per hour).
- **VPC basics:** public subnets hold the ALB (and NAT); private subnets hold tasks, database and Redis; security groups allow only the necessary ports (ALB to task, task to DB, task to Redis). Tasks need egress to the model provider via NAT, or to Bedrock via a VPC endpoint.
- **Quotas and throttling:** model providers return 429 or throttling errors. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `Retry-After`, cap total retries, and put a concurrency limit (semaphore) around model calls so you do not stampede yourself.

## Decision guide

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Streaming chat API, steady traffic | Fargate behind ALB |
| Rare webhook or S3-triggered glue | Lambda |
| Ingest thousands of documents | S3 -> SQS -> Fargate workers, DLQ, idempotent handlers |
| Same questions repeat, answers not user-specific | Exact-match cache with TTL |
| Answers depend on user permissions | Scope in key, or do not cache |
| You must not double-execute a tool call | Idempotency key with Postgres or Redis NX |
| Need AWS-native auth and data residency | Bedrock |
| Need the newest model feature | Provider API, key in Secrets Manager |

## Common failure modes

1. **Cross-user cache leak**: key lacks the permission scope.
2. **Stale answer after document edit**: TTL only, no generation bump.
3. **Cache stampede**: a hot key expires and 200 requests recompute at once; fix with single-flight and jittered TTLs.
4. **Redis outage becomes full outage**: no timeout, no fallback.
5. **Retry storm**: every worker retries the provider at the same moment; add jitter and a concurrency cap.
6. **Poison message**: one bad PDF fails forever and blocks throughput; DLQ after a few receives.
7. **Over-broad IAM**: `s3:*` on `*`; one prompt-injection-driven bug becomes a data breach.
8. **Unbounded cost**: no per-tenant token limit, no alarm.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The sketch put the RAG API on a public subnet with a wide-open security group 'for testing', IAM on a shared key, and Redis as a session dump of full prompts including customer text. Rate limiting was 'we'll add CloudFront later'. When the provider timed out, the client retried without an idempotency key and double-wrote a ticket. The runbook did not say who owns the cache flush.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'Redis is evicting keys. What did you store, and what is safe to drop?' Outline: cache model completions and retrieval by content hash; do not put secrets or the only copy of a write in Redis. Follow-up: 'Least privilege for the task role?' Answer: invoke the specific model, read the specific bucket prefix, connect to the specific Redis; no `*` on IAM.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a second region and a homemade queue. Keep a private API, one IAM role, Redis for cache/rate/idempotency, and a dependency-down path.

## The exercise

**Practice:** the practical level of AWS and Redis for an AI service. **Artifact:** a short architecture + runbook note for deploying a RAG or agent API on AWS with Redis in front of the model provider. The code below is the tested part of that note: three Redis patterns you can run offline, plus the IAM policy for the task role.

You will build, in order:

1. `fake_redis.py`: a tiny in-memory object with the same method names as redis-py (`get`, `set(ex, nx)`, `incr`, `expire`, `delete`) and an injectable clock, so TTL tests need no sleeping. In production you swap in `redis.Redis(...)`.
2. `ai_cache.py`: a tenant-namespaced response cache with TTL, generation-based invalidation, an access scope in the key, single-flight, and graceful degradation.
3. `guards.py`: a token-bucket limiter (with the real Lua script) and an idempotency-key decorator.
4. `test_ai_redis.py`: pytest tests for every behaviour you will be asked about in an interview.
5. `task-role.tf`: the least-privilege task role.

Run: `pip install pytest` then `pytest -q` in the folder. Seven tests should pass.

## Walkthrough

### The fake

`FakeRedis` stores strings and an expiry time per key, and purges lazily on access, as real Redis effectively does from the caller's view. Two switches matter for tests: `clock` (advance time by assigning `clock.t`) and `down` (raise `ConnectionError` on every call, which is what redis-py raises when it cannot connect). Its `token_bucket` method is a Python mirror of the Lua script, because a fake cannot run Lua. That is a real limitation: the fake proves the *algorithm and the call pattern*, not the Lua syntax. Before shipping, run the script once against a real Redis (a local container is enough) in an integration test.

### The cache

Look at `make_key`: `app:{tenant}:g{generation}:{kind}:{scope}:{digest}`.

- **tenant** prevents cross-tenant hits.
- **generation** is the invalidation lever. `invalidate_tenant` is one `INCR`; every key written under the old generation is unreachable immediately and expires by TTL. No `SCAN`, no `DEL` of thousands of keys.
- **scope** is the caller's access scope (`user:42` or `acl:<hash of sorted group ids>`). Two users with different permissions can never read each other's cached answer. If the answer is not user-specific (public docs), pass a constant scope like `public`.
- **digest** is a SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the payload (question, prompt version, model, retrieved ids). Sorted keys give a stable hash.

`get_or_compute` reads the generation and the key inside one `try`. A `ConnectionError` there means "Redis is unavailable", so it calls `compute()` directly and counts a degraded call. After a miss, the first caller becomes the **leader** for that key (a dictionary of in-flight records guarded by a mutex); followers wait on an event and reuse the leader's value. This is single-flight inside one process. Across many containers you still get at most one compute per container per key, which is usually enough; if not, add a short `SET NX` lock and accept its pitfalls from the concepts part. The write back to Redis is also wrapped, because a failure to cache must never fail the user's request.

### The limiter

`LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET` reads tokens and timestamp from a hash, refills `elapsed * rate` capped at capacity, spends `cost` if enough, writes back, sets an `EXPIRE` of twice the full-refill time so idle buckets disappear, and returns 1 or 0. Because Redis runs a script atomically, two concurrent requests cannot both spend the last token. Time comes from `redis.call('TIME')`, so container clock skew does not matter. `fail_open=True` returns "allowed" when Redis is down; for an expensive endpoint set `fail_open=False`. In the test: capacity 3, rate 1 per second gives three allowed then one denied, a second user has an independent bucket, and after advancing the clock 2 seconds two more are allowed.

For LLM cost control pass `cost` as an estimated token count and use `capacity` as a tokens-per-minute budget; settle the difference after the call.

### Idempotency

`Idempotency.run` does `SET key pending NX EX lock_ttl`. The winner runs `fn`; on success it overwrites the key with the stored result for `ttl` (a day); on exception it **deletes** the key so the client can retry safely. A loser reads the record: a different body fingerprint raises `KeyReuse`, a still-pending record raises `InProgress` (map to HTTP 409), and a finished record returns the stored result. The decorator form wraps `fn(tenant, body)` into `fn(tenant, idem_key, body)`.

Honest limit: if the process dies after performing the side effect but before saving the result, a retry after `lock_ttl` runs the side effect again. For money or email use the downstream system's own idempotency key too, or record the effect in Postgres in the same transaction.

### The IAM policy

The Terraform document gives the task role five statements: read objects only under `tenants/`, list the bucket only for that prefix, consume (not send to) the ingest queue, invoke exactly the chat and embedding models, and read exactly one secret. No wildcards on resources. Logs are not here: that belongs to the execution role. If you use a customer-managed KMS key, add `kms:Decrypt` on that key only. Bedrock resource ARNs differ for inference profiles and regions; **check current docs** for the exact ARN form for your models. Test a policy with the IAM policy simulator and by trying a forbidden call in staging.

## Turning this into the artifact

Your one-page note should have: the architecture diagram; a table of components with the reason for each; the Redis key schema (`app:{tenant}:g{n}:{kind}:{scope}:{digest}`, `rl:{tenant}:{user}`, `idem:{tenant}:{key}`); TTLs and the eviction policy; the failure table (Redis down, provider down, queue backlog); an alarm list; and a rollback step. The runbook section should read like instructions to a tired on-call engineer: symptom, check, action.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The sketch put the RAG API on a public subnet with a wide-open security group 'for testing', IAM on a shared key, and Redis as a session dump of full prompts including customer text. Rate limiting was 'we'll add CloudFront later'. When the provider timed out, the client retried without an idempotency key and double-wrote a ticket. The runbook did not say who owns the cache flush.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'Redis is evicting keys. What did you store, and what is safe to drop?' Outline: cache model completions and retrieval by content hash; do not put secrets or the only copy of a write in Redis. Follow-up: 'Least privilege for the task role?' Answer: invoke the specific model, read the specific bucket prefix, connect to the specific Redis; no `*` on IAM.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut a second region and a homemade queue. Keep a private API, one IAM role, Redis for cache/rate/idempotency, and a dependency-down path.

import hashlib
import json

LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET = """
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = tonumber(t[1]) + tonumber(t[2]) / 1000000
local rate, cap, cost = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
local s = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens, ts = tonumber(s[1]), tonumber(s[2])
if tokens == nil then tokens = cap; ts = now end
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate) * 2)
return allowed
"""


class TokenBucketLimiter:
    """With real redis-py: self.script = redis.register_script(LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET)
    and allow() calls self.script(keys=[key], args=[rate, capacity, cost])."""

    def __init__(self, redis, rate, capacity, fail_open=True, prefix="rl"):
        self.r = redis
        self.rate = rate
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.fail_open = fail_open
        self.prefix = prefix

    def allow(self, tenant, user, cost=1):
        key = f"{self.prefix}:{tenant}:{user}"
        try:
            return self.r.token_bucket(key, self.rate, self.capacity, cost) == 1
        except ConnectionError:
            return self.fail_open


class InProgress(Exception):
    pass


class KeyReuse(Exception):
    pass


class Idempotency:
    def __init__(self, redis, ttl=86400, lock_ttl=120, prefix="idem"):
        self.r = redis
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.lock_ttl = lock_ttl
        self.prefix = prefix

    def run(self, tenant, idem_key, body, fn):
        key = f"{self.prefix}:{tenant}:{idem_key}"
        fp = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        pending = json.dumps({"state": "pending", "fp": fp})
        if self.r.set(key, pending, ex=self.lock_ttl, nx=True):
            try:
                result = fn(body)
            except Exception:
                self.r.delete(key)  # let the client retry
                raise
            done = json.dumps({"state": "done", "fp": fp, "result": result})
            self.r.set(key, done, ex=self.ttl)
            return result
        saved = json.loads(self.r.get(key) or pending)
        if saved["fp"] != fp:
            raise KeyReuse("idempotency key reused with a different body")
        if saved["state"] == "pending":
            raise InProgress("original request still running")
        return saved["result"]


def idempotent(store):
    """Decorator for fn(tenant, idem_key, body)."""
    def wrap(fn):
        def inner(tenant, idem_key, body):
            return store.run(tenant, idem_key, body, lambda b: fn(tenant, b))
        return inner
    return wrap
